title: The Faithful Typewriter
premise: In the final winter of the Great War, Juniper Voss, a nurse in a requisitioned French village hospital, secretly records in her typewritten ledger the names of wounded soldiers the officers' official reports omit — deserters, colonial troops, and one German prisoner, Elias Brandt, who once saved her brother's life in peacetime. When army inspectors arrive to audit records and purge 'enemy sympathies,' her ledger becomes evidence of treason, and Juniper must choose between loyalty to the found family of nurses who sheltered her and the truth she promised to carry for Elias. She smuggles the ledger out during an armistice-eve bombing, testifies before a tribunal at great personal cost, and secures Elias's release; the book ends with the armistice signed and Juniper, no longer hiding behind busy hands, reading the names aloud at a memorial where both sides are counted.
about_author: Rosalind Ashgrove is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing wartime correspondence in regional hospital collections. She writes historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Ledger Under the Floorboard
chapters.summary: Juniper Voss, POV. In a requisitioned French château turned hospital, Juniper types official reports by day and secretly records omitted names by night — including German prisoner Elias Brandt, who tends the garden and once saved her brother. Emotional beat: quiet vigilance and the comfort of secret purpose.

chapters.title: Names That Don't Count
chapters.summary: Juniper, POV. A convoy of colonial troops arrives; their casualties vanish from official rolls, and Juniper adds them to her ledger while befriending Sister Marguerite and orderly Tomás, her found family. Emotional beat: belonging deepens even as the injustice sharpens.

chapters.title: A Promise Made in Peacetime
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through present scenes, Juniper's POV. We learn how Elias saved her brother Heinrich before the war in Leipzig, and the promise she made: his name would be remembered as a man, not an enemy. Emotional beat: tenderness shadowed by dread of what war demands.

chapters.title: The Requisition
chapters.summary: Juniper, POV. Captain Aldous Reeve arrives to requisition the town's remaining supplies and audit all records; the ledger's existence is nearly discovered when he commandeers the typing room. Emotional beat: fear tightening into resolve.

chapters.title: What the Officers Omit
chapters.summary: Tomás, POV. Ordered to burn 'irregular' paperwork, Tomás discovers duplicates of Juniper's omissions and quietly returns them to her, binding himself to her risk. Emotional beat: complicity as an act of love.

chapters.title: Elias Is Declared Enemy
chapters.summary: Juniper, POV. Reeve classifies all German prisoners for transfer to a detention camp; Elias's protection by the matron collapses, and Juniper realizes only documented testimony of his peacetime act can save him. Emotional beat: desperation meeting duty.

chapters.title: The Audit
chapters.summary: Sister Marguerite, POV. The inspection begins; Marguerite lies beautifully to protect Juniper but is caught concealing documents, and the ledger is seized as evidence of treason against the nurses collectively. Emotional beat: loyalty tested against truth — which truth, whose loyalty?

chapters.title: Armistice Eve
chapters.summary: Juniper, POV. As shelling nears the village on rumors of imminent armistice, Juniper breaks into the records office during a bombardment to steal back the ledger, wounded in the attempt, with Tomás covering her escape. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into courage.

chapters.title: The Tribunal
chapters.summary: Juniper, POV. Before a hasty military tribunal, Juniper reads the ledger aloud — every omitted name, ending with Elias's account of saving Heinrich Voss — forcing Reeve to choose between procedure and shame. Emotional beat: climax; truth spoken plainly at last.

chapters.title: All the Names
chapters.summary: Juniper, POV. The armistice is signed; Elias is released, Marguerite cleared, and Juniper organizes a memorial where she reads every name from her ledger, both sides together. Emotional beat: grief and belonging resolved — she belongs not by hiding, but by bearing witness.
